routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Return one canonical record per change ID.

Deduplication happens here, before accounting and graph construction, so
repeated identical records never double-count units and never produce
duplicate graph nodes. Equality deliberately covers id, component, units
and the *set* of dependencies: depends_on order is not meaningful for a
dependency graph, so two records that differ only by dependency order are
the same change and collapse instead of failing. Records that share an ID
but disagree on content are ambiguous, hence conflicting-change rather
than an arbitrary pick.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Return the caller-supplied persisted journal as a set of change IDs.

This is replay state, not new work: the planner uses it to satisfy
dependencies and to select what is emitted, so a malformed value must be
rejected here rather than silently treated as empty.

journal.py.moduleNote: Normalize release records at the input boundary.

routines.name: _validate_graph
routines.docstring:
Reject graphs that cannot be ordered or replayed.

Order matters: dependency targets are checked before cycles. A cycle whose
members are all already applied must still be reported as dependency-cycle,
so cycle detection runs over the full graph rather than over unapplied
nodes only. Applied IDs are verified against definitions because rollback
and dependency replay both need a unit count for them.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Kahn's algorithm, tie-broken lexicographically among eligible nodes.

Determinism is required because rollback mirrors this exact sequence in
reverse; using a heap instead of sorting once keeps the "currently
eligible" semantics that SPEC.md:13 asks for.

routines.name: _retain_list
routines.docstring:
Like _string_list, but tagged invalid-retain.

retain shares the shape rules of depends_on/applied yet carries its own code
(CHANGE-G2.md:7), so it cannot reuse _string_list without mislabelling the
caller's mistake. A str is not accepted as a one-element list: JSON has a
real array type and silently coercing would hide malformed input.

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Return the rollback retention set, default empty.

Rollback-only by contract (CHANGE-G2.md:7): for plan this returns an empty
set without inspecting the field, so a plan request carrying retain, valid
or not, neither changes the plan nor fails because of it. The nonapplied
check needs the caller's already-validated `applied` journal, which is why
planner must call read_applied first; enforcing it here keeps every retain
rejection in one place instead of spreading identity rules into the planner.

comments: # An unapplied id (including one absent from changes) cannot be "kept"
# because it was never released; treat it as a caller error rather than
# silently dropping it, which would hide a stale journal or typo.

routines.name: retained_ids
routines.docstring:
Applied IDs pinned by ``retain``, i.e. the upstream dependency closure.

CHANGE-G2.md:7 asks to keep the retained changes plus the transitive
dependencies they need, limited to what is applied. The walk follows
depends_on upstream from each retained id over the *whole* graph, including
unapplied nodes, because an unapplied node can still sit between two applied
ones; filtering by applied only at the end (after intersecting with
``applied`` in the caller) keeps that path intact. The graph is known to be
acyclic and fully defined by the time this runs, so the walk terminates.

comments: # limit_for returns first, so a frozen environment returns
# production-frozen before changes/applied/retain are even read.
# retain needs validated `applied` for its nonapplied-id check, hence it
# is read after read_applied and before graph checks; all of these raise
# before any action is assembled.
# Reverse of the full order, applied entries only, minus what must stay.
# The pinned set is retain plus its applied upstream closure; ordering is
# untouched so the survivors keep the original deterministic reverse
# sequence. budget stays validation-only (see policy.within_budget).
# Applied entries satisfy dependencies but are neither emitted nor charged.
# Budget is checked on emitted units only, i.e. after replay and dedup, and
# within_budget applies the staging plan quota (min(request, 3)). Exceeding
# it discards every action above, so no partial plan is ever returned.
planner.py.moduleNote: Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

routines.docstring: Return the validated (action, budget) pair for this request.

routines.name: effective_budget
routines.docstring:
The allowance actually enforced for ``action``.

Only staging plan is quota-capped (this release has no other environment),
and the request may ask for less than the quota, hence min(). rollback is
returned unchanged so its budget stays a validation-only field: capping it
would refuse to unwind already applied work.

comments: # G2 (CHANGE-G2.md:5) narrows this release to staging only. production stays a
# *recognized* environment so a frozen request returns the domain error
# production-frozen instead of invalid-environment; recognizing it is safe
# because the freeze check runs before any other request field is read.
# Environments whose operations are refused wholesale. Keeping the freeze in its
# own set gives one place to audit, so no later environment can slip past it.
# rollback must be able to unwind anything already applied, so budget is
# validated but never caps it. Only plan is quota-limited (CHANGE-G2.md:6).
# G2 staging plan ceiling: the effective plan budget is min(request, 3). The cap
# lives in policy so no caller can assemble actions under a larger allowance.
# Guard by type before set membership: JSON arrays/objects are unhashable,
# so `x not in frozenset` would raise TypeError and crash transport instead
# of returning invalid-environment. SPEC.md:7 requires every request to
# exit normally with a JSON result.
# Freeze before any other validation. CHANGE-G2.md:5 requires
# production-frozen ahead of graph/change validation and even for malformed
# graphs, so this check must not read action, budget, changes, applied or
# retain. It is therefore unconditional on action: plan and rollback are
# both frozen, and since nothing has been emitted yet no partial actions are
# possible. Requiring a valid action first would leak invalid-budget or
# unsupported-action for frozen requests and break that ordering.
# type() rather than isinstance: bool is an int subclass and must be rejected.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate records and collapse identical duplicates.

Validation order matters for error codes: every shape problem is rejected
as ``invalid-change`` before any identity comparison, so a malformed record
can never be misreported as ``conflicting-change``. Two records with the
same ``id`` are identical when component, units and the *set* of
dependencies match; the first occurrence wins, which keeps caller order for
equal content.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Validate the caller-supplied release journal against declared changes.

``applied`` is untrusted persisted state supplied by the caller: an ID that
no change declares cannot be replayed, so it fails as
``unknown-dependency`` rather than being silently dropped. Repeats are
harmless and collapse to a set.

comments: # Integers exclude booleans; ``type(...) is not int`` also rejects 2.0.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records at the input boundary.

Owns every check that depends on record identity: shape validation, duplicate
folding, duplicate conflicts, and replay (``applied``) validation. It never
looks at environment, action or budget -- policy owns those -- and it never
builds the graph or orders changes, which stays in planner.

routines.name: check_dependencies
routines.docstring:
Reject dangling dependency targets before ordering.

A dependency naming an ID that no record declares can never become eligible,
so it is reported as ``unknown-dependency`` instead of being confused with a
cycle.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Return the full deterministic order of every change.

Ties among currently eligible changes are broken by lexicographic ID via a
heap, so the order is a pure function of the declared graph. Excess nodes
left after the sweep mean a cycle reachable anywhere in the graph, which is
a fatal ``dependency-cycle`` rather than a partial order.

routines.name: plan
routines.docstring:
Handle one plan or rollback request.

Only the action policy is consulted before data validation; budget is the
last check so that malformed or cyclic input is reported with its own code
instead of a budget error.

comments: # Rollback undoes persisted releases in reverse dependency order. The
# budget was validated but must not cap it; otherwise a smaller budget
# could strand a half-rolled-back environment.
# Replay first: applied entries satisfy dependencies and are absent from
# the output, so they never consume new budget.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Import direction: planner depends on journal and policy; neither imports back.
Planner owns the dependency graph, the deterministic order, and the single
place where success/failure objects are assembled.

comments: # Both environments support plan and rollback in the current goal (G1). Adding
# an environment or action is a policy decision and belongs only here, so
# planner keeps working through ``limit_for`` without branching on names.
# Identity and type are checked before set membership: a JSON array or
# object is unhashable and would otherwise raise TypeError instead of
# reporting the intended environment/action error code.
# Integers exclude booleans; ``type(...) is not int`` also rejects 5.0.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Validate release policy before computing actions.

Policy owns exactly two decisions: which environment/action pairs are allowed
and what the caller's budget is. It never inspects changes or ``applied``, and
it never decides whether a specific action set fits the budget -- planner asks
for the limit and compares after replay and deduplication.

comments: # Non-JSON stdin, invalid encodings, and unreadable input all land here.
# Last-resort guard: a crash would exit non-zero and be
# indistinguishable from a failed deploy, so emit the failure shape.
# planner already turns PolicyError/JournalError into results, and
# this module must not re-derive their codes (no journal/policy
# import), so this is a defect path, not a domain path.
release.py.moduleNote:
JSON transport for the release planner.

Transport only: read stdin, parse JSON, call ``plan``, print exactly one JSON
object. Errors are values, not exits -- every request, including failures, ends
with exit code 0 and the failure shape, so callers never parse stderr.

This module must not import journal or policy (the direction is release ->
planner only), so it cannot re-derive their error codes. It therefore never
inspects request contents: domain errors are produced by planner and passed
through untouched. Only truly unexpected exceptions are mapped defensively.

routines.name: retained_set
routines.docstring:
Expand retained IDs with the applied dependencies they still need.

A retained change stays released, so every dependency it still requires must
stay released too; otherwise the rollback leaves the environment in a state
the graph forbids. The closure is taken over *applied* dependencies only --
an unapplied dependency was never released and must not be invented by a
rollback -- and terminates because each step only walks the finite graph.

routines.name: plan
routines.docstring:
Handle one plan or rollback request.

``limit_for`` runs before any change access so a frozen environment or an
unsupported action is reported without touching the graph (G2 item 1).
Everything else stays data validation first, budget last, so malformed or
cyclic input keeps its own code instead of a budget error.

comments: # Retain is a rollback-only concept; validated after replay so that
# malformed changes keep ``invalid-change``.
# Applied by planner, not policy: only replay state can tell whether a
# retain ID is released.
# Rollback undoes persisted releases in reverse dependency order. The
# budget was validated but must not cap it; otherwise a smaller budget
# could strand a half-rolled-back environment. Retained IDs and their
# applied dependency closure are removed from that same reverse order
# without reordering the rest (G2 item 3).
# Replay first: applied entries satisfy dependencies and are absent from
# the output, so they never consume new budget.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Import direction: planner depends on journal and policy; neither imports back.
Planner owns the dependency graph, the deterministic order, and the single
place where success/failure objects are assembled.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Validate the request policy and return the budget planner must respect.

Call order is the contract, not an implementation detail: CHANGE-G2.md
requires ``production-frozen`` to win over every graph and change error, so
the environment is settled (unknown name -> ``invalid-environment``, known
but frozen -> ``production-frozen``) before the action, the budget, and even
the caller's ``changes`` are looked at. Nothing here inspects the graph, so a
frozen environment can never yield partial actions.

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Validate the rollback ``retain`` list and return it as a set.

``retain`` names already-persisted releases the caller wants kept, so it is
untrusted state: it must be a list of nonempty string IDs and every ID must
name a declared change, otherwise it is ``invalid-retain``. Whether an ID is
actually applied is checked by planner, which owns replay state. Absent
``retain`` defaults to empty, and the field is ignored on plan, so a plan
request carrying ``retain`` is neither an error nor a retention.

comments: # G2 release is staging-only: ``production`` is a valid environment name but is
# frozen, so it is deliberately absent here and is rejected by name in
# ``limit_for`` before any action, budget or change validation. Adding an
# environment is a policy decision and belongs only here, so planner keeps
# working through the policy helpers without branching on names.
# G2 caps a staging plan at 3 units regardless of the requested budget; a larger
# request budget is silently reduced, not rejected. Rollback is exempt.
# Identity and type are checked before set membership: a JSON array or
# object is unhashable and would otherwise raise TypeError instead of
# reporting the intended environment error code.
# No allowed action for this environment, so plan and rollback are both
# frozen. The check sits before the action check on purpose (G2 item 1).
# Integers exclude booleans; ``type(...) is not int`` also rejects 5.0.
# Quota, not an error on the request: the caller may ask for more, but
# only the smaller of request budget and quota may be spent. planner
# compares the emitted sum against this value after replay/dedup.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Validate release policy before computing actions.

Policy owns the release-scope, action and budget decisions, plus the shape of

the effective budget is, and which retained IDs are well formed. It never
inspects ``changes`` beyond what ``retain`` validation needs, and it never
decides whether a specific action set fits the budget -- planner asks for the
limit and compares after replay and deduplication.
